articles.title: Arthur Fery: British No 1 heads into American hard-court swing with areas he can improve ahead of US Open, according to Tim Henman
articles.summary: Tim Henman looks ahead to what's to come for new British No 1 Arthur Fery as the 24-year-old from Wimbledon prepares for the US Open; watch the ATP, WTA Tours and US Open from Aug 30 live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
The wild card's surprise run to the Wimbledon semi-finals has injected a much-needed shot of positivity and given British fans a new name to follow in the Grand Slams - starting at the US Open in New York - live on Sky Sports Tennis from August 30.

The challenge for the 24-year-old now is to acclimatise to his new standing in the game and the loss of anonymity and the freedom that brings with it.

The 23-year-old, who has soared to 36 in the world from No 114, was the last player standing in what was an otherwise dismal tournament for the host nation, but he became only the fifth British man this century to reach the second week at the All England Club.

Fery has earned direct entry to a Masters event for the first time in Cincinnati - 13-23 August - before appearing at the Winston-Salem Open from 23-29 August ahead of his debut at Flushing Meadows.

Speaking at Royal Birkdale ahead of The Open, Henman called Fery's dream run at the All England Club "amazing" and "transformational for his career and his life".

The former British No 1 said: "He started the year at 185 in the world, qualified in Melbourne and then has continued to improve his ranking - then getting a wild card at Wimbledon ranked 114 and winning five matches getting to the semi-finals it was an incredible performance - and I think it also shows the fine margins between these top players.

"If you're in the top 250 in the world you're an extremely good player and on your day you've got a chance of beating anyone, so huge for him to be 36 in the world now getting to the other Grand Slams and Masters 1000, so he's got an opportunity to really plan his schedule moving forward."

With July 20 rankings being used for the US Open main draw, it means Fery has no time to improve his current ranking of No 36, but a few withdrawals could help him nudge into a seeding position, which would be a massive boost.

"I mean it's interesting that actually the ranking points will come on after Wimbledon and then the entries are six weeks out so I think the first tournament he will take advantage of that is Cincinnati," explained Henman.

The 2004 US Open semi-finalist also believes Fery will only improve his overall power in order to compete with top-tier opponents.

"He's still got a lot of areas that he can improve in his game and I think that's exciting when you know you're young," said Henman. "I can't wait to watch him we need those British players at the top of the game and yeah he's got a great opportunity.

"We needed that because those first couple of days were pretty rough for British tennis, but it was brilliant to see Arthur play so well and if Emma [Raducanu] and Jack [Draper] can be back fit, then there's also Katie Boulter, Cam Norrie, while Jan Choinski has just broken into the top 100 - he's 75 in the world now - so you want those British players creating stories at the biggest events."

Fery ready for 'attention' like Raducanu after Wimbledon run

Fery admits he might be plunged into the media spotlight in a similar manner to Raducanu following his fairy tale run at Wimbledon.

"Yes, even already a little bit during the tournament I was thinking of life after and how I was going to handle all that because we've seen it with people who've broken through in that manner before," Fery told Sky News' Jacquie Beltrao.

"With Emma obviously, Emma won a Slam and I didn't but there was still a lot of media attention.

"It is going to be really important to handle that - the expectation from myself and also the public."

The Brit is ready for more time in the media glare as he competes against the top players in tennis.

"It means I can play the top players week in week out and compare myself to them and keep working on my tennis," said Fery.

"I am going to have to get accustomed to the full life of tour with more media attention and all of that but I think I'm ready for it.

"It is going to be a first as well playing the US Open. I didn't even play qualifiers last year so it's going be a great experience."

He is also relaxed about the possibility of being among the top-32 seeded players for Flushing Meadows.

"I might already be in there [the top 32] if I'm lucky, a few withdrawals," said Fery.

"I don't think I will be able to contribute to the ranking anymore before the list comes out for the US Open, because it's going to come out soon.

"Being seeded obviously protects you a little bit from the top guys, but it's my first main draw that I qualify for directly with my ranking so just going to take it as it goes."

articles.title: Emma Raducanu: British No 1 could end her season after US Open withdrawal with stress fracture
articles.summary: Emma Raducanu will skip the US Open due to a stress fracture, and Annabel Croft says Brit could forego the rest of the season;watch the ATP and WTA Tours and US Open from August 30 live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
The 23-year-old suffered a stress fracture to her right lower leg during the grass-court season and made a late decision to pull out of Wimbledon.

And following consultation with her medical team, Raducanu on Monday concluded she will be unable to play at the US Open later this month - live on Sky Sports .

Raducanu has only recently taken her first tentative steps back on court while wearing a protective boot, and the latest setback is another blow for the Brit after a frustrating 12 months plagued by persistent physical issues.

Speaking on Sky Sports Tennis , former player-turned-TV analyst Croft admitted "she's been unbelievably unlucky with injury problems."

"There are so many injuries out there but it seems like she never gets a clear run where she's able to really go for it with her tennis and her body and her mind and everything injury free and just keep the momentum going."

After a foot injury severely hampered her pre-season training, Raducanu then spent two-and-a-half months off court with a post-viral illness after initially falling unwell in early February.

She finally returned for the end of the clay-court season having rehired Andrew Richardson, the coach who guided her to the US Open title, but the pair's time on court together has been limited.

Raducanu enjoyed one of the best weeks of her career by reaching her biggest final since New York at Queen's Club in June but it was that effort that triggered her latest setback.

"I've seen lots of pictures of her posting with the boot on her leg and just trying to serve, to keep her racket going and showing everybody that she's doing everything she can. But clearly, it's not healed up," said Croft, who retired from the professional tour at the age of 21.

There will now be question marks over whether Raducanu, who will slide from her current ranking of 49, will compete again in 2026 with the temptation of a protected ranking.

Should she miss at least six months of competition due to injury, she can use a special ranking for a select number of events upon her return. This would be her top-50 ranking from during the grass season - the last time she competed and received prize money for a tournament.

Raducanu is at the risk of dropping down the rankings with a lot of points to defend following last year's north American hard-court swing in Washington, Canada, Cincinnati, and the US Open.

"It wouldn't be a surprise if she made that decision [close down her season]," said Croft, a former world No 24. "That wouldn't be such a bad decision to take because you can fully heal, rest up, get as much treatment as possible and then come out fully fit, raring to go at the start of next year.

"Maybe if there's a worry about the ranking drop with so many points to defend and potentially that ranking could plummet, although she might benefit from the protected ranking.

"All of these factors have to be considered, don't they? But at the end of the day, your health is your wealth, as they say, and that is the most important factor and she just needs to get herself fit.

"It's an unusual injury. I mean, I've had calf muscle injuries, which were not nice at all. And the minute you push off, you tweak it and it feels tight but the one thing that I've always thought about Raducanu, particularly when we saw her at Queen's Club on the grass where she played such beautiful tennis, is that she's very light on her feet. Movement has always been one of her strengths.

"She's such a great athlete. She moves around the ball. She's light on her feet and gets into great positions where she never looks off balance. But movement will be part of a major strength of what she brings out onto the court. That needs to be absolutely 100 per cent."

articles.title: US Open key questions: Gigi Salmon dissects the draws with Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic, Aryna Sabalenka and Coco Gauff in the mix
articles.summary: Gigi Salmon dissects the men's and women's draws ahead of the US Open; who will the presenter pick as her winners for the titles in New York?; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
It's also played on a surface where more players fancy their chances; many have love-hate relationships with clay and grass but hard courts are their bread and butter.

The US Open is now a three-week event, week one is fan week, which this year saw five-time champion Roger Federer return for an exhibition, Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik win their first Grand Slam title after being crowned mixed doubles champions - in a competition that saw a return to Flushing Meadows of six-time champion Serena Williams - and the qualifying competition, which started with 15 Brits in the draw.

The main draw starts on Sunday and contains nine Brits, with a record five coming through qualifying. The men's competition is headed up by Sascha Zverev in the absence of Jannik Sinner [knee injury] and the women's by world No 1 Aryna Sabalenka.

In terms of questions to be asked, there are five main ones...

How will the wrist of returning champion Carlos Alcaraz hold up under the pressure of best-of-five-set Grand Slam play?

Will 39-year-old Novak Djokovic finally get his hands on Grand Slam title No 25?

Can an American finally win the men's title in New York? The last to do it was Andy Roddick in 2003.

Can Aryna Sabalenka make history and win the US Open title for a third consecutive year? It's something that hasn't been done since Serena Williams in 2012-14.

And maybe more importantly... who will end the tournament as world No 1, with four players in the running?

If we break down the draws starting with the men, the top half is headed up in the absence of Sinner by Zverev, top seed at a Grand Slam for the first time and with a major title under his belt having won the French Open earlier this year.

The draw has been kind to the German, who will fancy his chances and comes into the tournament with an 18-2 record at Grand Slam level this year.

The question, as always, is how will he cope with the pressure having fallen early in both Masters 1000 events in the lead-up as the top seed.

Working from top to bottom, the second quarter is headed up by the Australian and sixth seed Alex de Minaur, projected to meet Zverev in the quarter-finals. He might not have Djokovic or Alcaraz in his section but he does have former finalist Taylor Fritz, French Open finalist Flavio Cobolli and last year's semi-finalist Felix Auger-Aliassime.

The bottom half is absolutely stacked and features all five former US Open champions in Alcaraz, Djokovic, Daniil Medvedev, Stan Wawrinka and Marin Cilic.

Working our way down next up is Djokovic's quarter, which features Medvedev, finalist in Cincinnati Francis Tiafoe, finalist in Canada Brandon Nakashima, and a second-round meeting with one of Wawrinka or Matteo Berrettini. That's before any talk of a meeting with Alcaraz - the defending champion who heads up the final quarter.

The seeds in the Alcaraz section include winner in Canada, Ben Shelton, winner in Cincinnati, Arthur Fils, Alexander Bublik, Tommy Paul and big-hitting Roman Safiullin, who has beaten him before and is, for me, one of his toughest tests for the Spaniard having not played a singles match since April.

Into the women's draw with each quarter containing very different stories...

The main story involving Sabalenka in the first quarter who is not only looking to try and become the first woman since Serena Williams to win three consecutive US Open titles but she's also trying to hold on to the world No 1 ranking.

On paper her draw isn't too bad until the quarter-finals, where she could face Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova.

The worry is Sabalenka's lack of form going 17-7 since April and not having won a title since March. She is without a Grand Slam title so far in 2026 and is looking vulnerable.

The second quarter is headlined by Jessica Pegula who is in contention to end the tournament as world No 1. For that to happen, the former finalist would need to win the title; nothing less would do.

Dangers lie around every corner for Pegula with Elina Svitolina, Karolina Muchova and Sorana Cirstea in her section and a second-round meeting with one of former Australian Open Champion Sofia Kenin or two-time US Open Champion Venus Williams.

Former US Open champion and current Cincinnati champion Coco Gauff heads up the top of the bottom half; she also has a chance of reaching world No 1, but only if she wins the title.

Lying in wait for her in the third quarter are last year's finalist Amanda Anisimova, French Open Champion Mirra Andreeva, Washington champion Alex Eala, and a potentially tricky early meeting with Paula Badosa.

And finally, to what surely is the toughest quarter of the draw with Elena Rybakina, Iga Swaitek, Naomi Osaka, Madison Keys and Belinda Bencic.

Rybakina will be the new world No 1 if she reaches the semi-finals, that is in her hands. What isn't is the left ankle/Achilles injury that she has been managing for a while, but flared up in Cincinnati forcing her to withdraw in her match against Swiatek. She has looked tentative in practice, so only time will tell if it will hold up to allow her to reach world No 1 for the first time in her career.

When it comes to the Brits, a word on Arthur Fery, who in his second tournament since reaching the semi-finals of Wimbledon this summer, reached the final of Winston-Salem - losing out to third seed Ignacio Buse in the title decider .

Perfect preparation for Fery who has had a whirlwind summer and now heads to New York as the British No 1 thanks to that run.

The Brit will be making his debut at the US Open and it's a tough one up against 13th seed Lorenzo Musetti.

Musetti recently found some form in Cincinnati but isn't long back from a back injury, so Fery will fancy his chances.

Fery sits in the top quarter draw with top seed Zverev. Also in that section is Jan Choinski, who takes on the Dutchman Botic Van De Zandschulp.

And the other Brit to qualify on ranking is Cameron Norrie, who is in the bottom half with Alcaraz. He is the 29th seed and faces the Frenchman Luca van Assche, for the right to take on Miomir Kecmanovic or Dennis Shapovalov in round two.

In total, there are nine Brits in the main draw and for the first time at the US Open five having come through qualifying.

Among them is Toby Samuel, the world No 110, who will make his US Open main draw debut, with the 23-year-old having drawn the Czech Tomas Machac, the world No 58.

Harry Wendleken is also set for his debut after playing nine sets and nine hours to reach the main draw, and his reward is the 21st seed Luciano Darderi. Jacob Fearnley, in as a lucky loser for his second US Open appearance, will take on the Spaniard Martin Landaluce.

In the women's draw, Katie Boulter was the only direct entrant and has been handed a good first round up against the American wild card Carol Young Suh Lee.

Lee is 24, sitting at her career-high ranking of 140, and will be making her Grand Slam main draw debut.

Should Boulter win, then more than likely she will face US Open mixed doubles champion and Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova in round two.

Joining Boulter through the qualifying route is Harriet Dart, who beat Heather Watson in the final round to set up a meeting with the American and world No 54 Peyton Stearns, who she recently played and lost to in Cincinnati, but did beat the American in US Open qualifying in 2021.

And Fran Jones, who for a second year running has secured qualification into the main draw where she will face Magda Linette of Poland in what will be a first meeting between the two.

Also a reminder that we haven't seen the last of Serena Williams at the US Open this year.

After playing with Alcaraz in the mixed doubles she is teaming up with sister Venus in the doubles after getting a wild card.

The two-time US Open doubles champions last played a Grand Slam together in 2022 at Flushing Meadows.

And just a word on the prize money, which has risen again this year: the men's and women's singles champions will get $5.5m (£4.7m) each and for reaching the first round it's a guaranteed $140,000 (£120,000).

I have left it as late as possible, and I'm still not convinced, but for who's going to win.

I will say Zverev to win his second Grand Slam title. It was tough to go against him once I saw what looks like a very favourable draw and for the women I am going outside of those who could end the tournament as world No 1 and pick Naomi Osaka to win her third US Open and first here since 2020.

From Sunday, the Sky Sports Tennis team will be back together for 15 days of wall-to-wall action with every ball of every match on every court available for you to enjoy.

Hear from Martin Navratilova, Tim Henman, Marion Bartoli, Laura Robson, Ryan Harrison and Naomi Broady to name just a few.

We look forward to your company this Sunday from 3pm live from New York.

articles.title: US Open: Ben Shelton beats Carlos Alcaraz in five-set thriller in latest-ever finish to US Open match at 3.33am
articles.summary: Ben Shelton clinches first-ever victory over top-three opponent as he beats Carlos Alcaraz to set up US Open semi-final showdown with Frances Tiafoe; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
The American prevailed 6-7 (5-7) 6-1 6-3 1-6 7-6 (10-7) over four hours and 28 minutes to reward a raucous Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd gripped until 3.33am in what was the latest-ever finish to a US Open match.

It marked Shelton's first career win over a top-three player, against which he had been 0-17 coming into the match.

Shelton will now play Frances Tiafoe in the final four after his fellow countryman's thrilling five-set victory over Alex Michelsen earlier in the evening.

"For me it's always about the people in the crowd, whether it's my coaches, team or friends and family, or the city of New York that showed up tonight until 3am with the USA chants, that's what kept me going and what got me this win," Shelton said on-court.

"It's incredible. This is the greatest sports city and greatest stadium in the world. I'm hoping my best friend and sister don't have to be at work at 6am.

"I'm so grateful, so blessed to be in front of you guys and share the court with Carlos is an absolute honour."

Shelton's victory means the United States is guaranteed representation in Sunday's men's final, with Andy Roddick the last American man to win a major title back in 2003.

It also spelled the end of Alcaraz's courageous return to the court having been out for more than four months with a wrist injury and initially been a doubt to compete in New York.

The seven-time major champion, playing his first tournament since April, was seen vomiting before the beginning of the final set, which culminated in a 10-point match-deciding tie-break.

"As I said before the tournament began, the expectation was to go there, compete... playing these kind of matches, for me being healthy," said Alcaraz. "It was close, it really was close. So I'm just a little bit disappointed, about, (not) getting the win at the end.

"But, I'm just happy, I'm just proud about myself, about how I fought. After the third set, physically I was really tired, but I found a way to push myself up, physically give an extra. In the fifth set

"I just started to feel better and better. I was playing against one of the... he is a beast. He's an unbelievable player. Powerful. He just managed how to play really, really well in every situation, so credit to him. I leave the court happy, I leave the court with a smile, healthy, and this is what I needed."

Shelton heads into his third Grand Slam semi-final having previously reached the final four of the 2023 US Open and the 2025 Australian Open.

Having lost the opening tie-break, the 23-year-old stormed to nine straight games on his way to dominant second and third sets. Back came Alcaraz to send it to a decider, where he would win four successive points to lead 5-3 in the tie-break before inviting Shelton to turn things around.

In true Shelton fashion, he iced the game with a serve of 146mph that Alcaraz failed to tame, bringing the New York crowd to their feet.

"I remember, the last tiebreak that I played was in Paris," recalled Alcaraz. "It was an unbelievable game that I played in that moment. This time, when you are trying to fight and trying to overcome all the problems you might have - physically, tired a lot, obviously when he's serving, he puts a lot of pressure on you.

"You're thinking about, trying to put the return in, and it's unknown if you're going to play the point or he's going to get a free point with the serve. I think in these moments he takes a lot of advantage with serve, but not any excuse, but I would say it's an important weapon in these moments."

Tiafoe reaches US Open semis in thrilling fightback

Frances Tiafoe recovered from two sets down and ‌erased a 0-3 deficit in the fifth set to beat American compatriot Alex Michelsen 5-7 3-6 7-5 6-3 7-6 (10-6), reaching the semi-finals for a third time.

The 11th seed ​appeared to have lost all the magic of his early campaign before claiming the momentum in the third set and clinching ​it with a forehand winner to the deafening cheers of ‌the fans on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Michelsen had flown under the radar in his deepest major run but ​earned respect on the biggest stage of American tennis with 21 aces, and Tiafoe cut his own celebration short to comfort the 22-year-old in an emotional ​embrace.

"I hope he gets tight," Tiafoe said of his mindset at 4-5 down in the third set. "He gave me some gifts, a couple of double faults there.

"But then I slowly started to get my rhythm there, snuck out the third set and slowly started playing better and better.

"He is a hell of a player. He should've easily won today, so shout out Alex Michelsen."

Tiafoe joined Andre Agassi as the only American men to reach three US Open semi-finals in this century and will return to the top 10 for the first time in three years in the rankings.

"Everyone was sleeping in the first couple of hours and I was asleep with you all," Tiafoe joked following his win.

"As it went along, the energy was incredible, as always. Thank you [to the crowd] for being there for me. I really appreciate that."

"You can't help but feel sorry for Alex Michelsen considering how close he was and we all know Frances is a fan favourite in this situation.

"The tears started coming from Michelsen. It was like a punch in the gut for me and I don't even know him.

"Having been in these situations when you're so close to the finishing line and you know it's on your racket, I think that's the worst feeling. You know that you kind of did choke a little bit. That's the absolute worst.

"Brutal day for him but you have to tip your cap to Frances for turning that match around."

articles.title: US Open: 3.33am local time and another early-morning finish as Ben Shelton beat Carlos Alcaraz, so does something have to change?
articles.summary: Ben Shelton beat Carlos Alcaraz 6-7 (5-7) 6-1 6-3 1-6 7-6 (10-7) in a match that started just after 11pm and ended at 3:33am Wednesday; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
Three long matches earlier on Tuesday meant Alcaraz and Shelton did not step on to court until gone 11pm .

The US Open craves its night matches and players love the energy the fans provide - even when a number of matches have already gone past 2am this year.

Thousands stayed to the end, with Arthur Ashe Stadium perhaps still one-third full for the finish. Shelton benefited from a home-crowd even against the popular Alcaraz, with fans chanting his name along with "USA! USA!"

"It's incredible," Shelton said. "I always say that this is the greatest sports city in the world, I say that this is the greatest stadium in the world. I'm just hoping that my best friend and my sister over there don't have to be at work at 6am in three hours."

But Martina Navratilova was not impressed at yet another early-morning finish, the former world No 1 posting on X: "Something has got to give - this is not OK and it is not normal - no other sport might start at 11AM or 11PM. In the same event."

So have we now reached an extreme? The early-morning finishes have stirred frustration and concerns about how organisers are managing the schedule at the Grand Slam event with numerous matches straying well past midnight.

The US Open took to social media with a light-hearted nod to the late night, offering a fill-in-the-blank letter for fans to ask their bosses to be excused from work on Wednesday.

"We understand how important showing up is, but sometimes you have to make time for things you're passionate about," the post on X stated. "Carlos Alcaraz and Ben Shelton put on an absolute stellar performance during their US Open quarterfinal, and ______ was a fully committed fan who was completely locked in from start to finish."

Speaking on the Served Podcast, host Andy Roddick defended the late-night finishes, saying: "I know a lot of the comments are, you know, 'How do you finish at 4 in the morning?' and all of that," he said.

"Well, every match goes to a match tie-break except for one. And you've got to get 25,000 people out of a stadium responsibly, and you've got to get 25,000 people in responsibly. So, I hear a lot of complaining. I don't hear a lot of proposed solutions."

What is the impact of late-night finishes?

Sleep schedules, meal times and warm-ups are all impacted by the ticking clock.

"When you finish late, the next day shifts a lot," Aryna Sabalenka said earlier in the tournament. "Like, you still need to get your hours of sleep, so you start later. You just can really mess up your schedule."

Sabalenka is not alone; Venus Williams also said it was "not ideal" that her match against Sofia Kenin last Monday didn't start until past midnight.

"I think it wasn't great for either of us, so I think we both tried our best," she said. "Yeah, I just don't know any other sport where you have to start that late. I definitely think there's room for improvement there."

Speaking on Sky Sports Tennis , coach Ryan Harrison said there's no solution to the late-night finishes while former Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli concluded: "From a TV point of view it's great because you have people on the edge of their sofa and they want to watch the match from home.

"But I will say, ultimately, one match a night especially when you get down to the quarter-finals and you know those matches are going to be a lot closer could potentially be the solution.

"I'd say in the first week you can have two matches because you know some of the matches might be one-sided, but as you move on, definitely one match."

articles.title: US Open: Top-seeded quartet set for women's semi-final showdown with Aryna Sabalenka and Coco Gauff in action
articles.summary: Hat-trick hunting Aryna Sabalenka takes on Jessica Pegula with new world No 1 Elena Rybakina facing home favourite Coco Gauff in the semi-finals; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
For the first time since Wimbledon in ​2009, all four top seeds at a Grand Slam have reached the semi-finals, with Sabalenka, Rybakina and Gauff all former major champions and third seed Pegula seeking a maiden Grand Slam title.

Sabalenka has reached the semi-finals here for a sixth consecutive year and is now two wins away from becoming the first woman ‌since Serena Williams from 2012 to 2014 to win three straight titles in New York.

The top seed had not dropped a set before surviving her toughest test of the tournament ​on Tuesday, edging Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova .

The Belarusian will face a familiar opponent in third seed Pegula, with their rivalry returning to Flushing Meadows for a third straight year after Sabalenka denied the American the title in 2024 and then beat her ​again in last year's semi-finals.

Sabalenka leads their head-to-head 9-4 but Pegula has won two of their last three ⁠encounters, including a victory in the Berlin Open semi-finals earlier this year ⁠in which she took the deciding set 6-0.

"I think it's fun to look at the rivalry we've had. She's got to me here the last couple of years," Pegula said.

"I have been able to beat ‌her a few times, maybe on a smaller stage, so I think that's going to be kind of a hurdle for me to get over."

Sabalenka will head into the semi-final after surrendering top spot in the world rankings, which Rybakina secured with her quarter-final victory over Olympic champion Qinwen Zheng.

The Australian Open winner will become the 30th woman to top the WTA rankings and the first from Kazakhstan to reach world No 1 when the new rankings are released after the ⁠tournament.

Sabalenka, who had held the top spot since October 2024, said she would gladly trade it for ​another US Open title.

"I'll be more than happy," she said. "Yes, three-peat. Sounds great."

New world No 1 up against the fan-favourite

Rybakina's reward for reaching the semi-finals for the first time in New York is a meeting with fan-favourite ​Gauff, who produced a stunning comeback to beat fifth seed and fellow French Open winner Mirra Andreeva .

The 2023 ⁠US Open champion was on the brink of defeat in the second set before saving two match points and turning the match around.

Gauff's victory put her into the semi-finals at a second straight Slam after her run to the last four at Wimbledon, and she will have the home crowd behind ⁠her as she bids to clinch a second US Open title.

"Elena is playing some great tennis," said Gauff. "Congrats to her for being the new world No 1 or will be the new World No 1. I think that's incredible.

"We played each other in Toronto. That didn't go my way, so I think I just have to learn from that match.

"I know I'm going to have some aces hit on me and some winners hit on me, but I'm going to keep fighting and give it my all."

A third Slam title or revenge for Gauff?

Rybakina will bid ​for a third Grand Slam title, while Gauff will have revenge on her mind after the Kazakh beat her in ​three sets in last month's Canadian Open semi-finals.

On playing Gauff, Rybakina said: "I will expect that a lot of people are going to support her.

"I just need to stay aggressive. I think from where I was coming to this tournament, being injured and not practicing, I think we came pretty far. Now we just last push and important to still enjoy. Hopefully it's going to go my way."

The pair are tied 1-1 in their previous meetings and will face off for a place in Saturday's final.

articles.title: US Open chief Craig Tiley tells Sky Sports Tennis he plans on keeping day and night format at Flushing Meadows in 2027
articles.summary: US Open chief Craig Tiley vows to keep same day and night format despite Ben Shelton beating Carlos Alcaraz at 3:33am local time; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
Tiley, who took the helm as new CEO of USTA earlier this year after leading Tennis Australia since 2013, says he has no plans for any changes to the schedule.

It comes after Ben Shelton's five-set thriller against Carlos Alcaraz in the quarter-finals ended at 3:33am local time on Wednesday, leaving few people awake to see the near five-hour marathon reach its finale on one of the sport's biggest stages.

Players have long loved the electricity of playing night matches under the lights in the nation's biggest city.

But the tournament had already set a record with three post-2am finishes over the first six days, as well as having two other matches go past 1am.

The issue ​has gained added resonance amid a broader push by top players for increased prize money and reforms on welfare ‌and working conditions, with late finishes emerging as a flashpoint in the debate over life on the tour.

Like the US Open, the Australian Open has faced criticism for notoriously late ​finishes but the other two Grand Slams have imposed checks, with Wimbledon halting play under an 11pm local curfew and the French Open limiting night sessions to one match.

Yet a solution such as starting evening sessions earlier than 7pm is complicated by the argument that ​tennis-mad New Yorkers need time to get to Flushing Meadows after work and organisers having to manage day-and night-session ⁠crowds.

Tiley said: "I hear from a lot of people that it finishes too late and then I say, okay, and your suggestion is? I don't get anything.

"You can't control the length of the match. What's really interesting is in the last 10 years the amount of tennis from when you hit a point to when a point stops has been about the same.

"But the length of the matches on the men's side has increased by an average of about 25 minutes. That's because we now have the shot clock so everyone is taking their time, and we have the towels here which takes a bit more time and so the whole length of it is a bit longer. Not that much longer, but in fact the average time of the men's matches today is still not in the top four average times in the last 10 years.

"While it feels really late, the reality is you've got to go and look at the data, But that being said, no one wants to finish at 3.30am in the morning, although the rest of the world in the daytime saw a pretty amazing match."

"We really like the two days and two nights. Two full sessions and you get a women's match and a great men's match, and that's what our fans are telling us. They can come out and see three, four, five hours of entertainment and if it goes really long like the other night, that's a great sporting ticket so I will keep it," Tiley added.

Just hours after the Shelton-Alcaraz match concluded, the US Open took to social media with a light-hearted nod to the late night, offering a fill-in-the-blank letter for fans to ask their bosses to be excused from work on Wednesday.

"We understand how important showing up is, but sometimes you have to make time for things you're passionate about," the post on X stated. "Carlos Alcaraz and Ben Shelton put on an absolute stellar performance during their US Open quarterfinal, and ______ was a fully committed fan who was completely locked in from start to finish."

Another suggestion that surfaces whenever late finishes dominate the conversation is reducing men's matches to best-of-three sets in the earlier rounds, though the idea is contentious among those who view five-set ⁠matches as central to Grand Slams.

"I think for the men's we should stick ​with three out of five," Frances Tiafoe said.

"I don't know where the conversation is going, what people ​are leaning to. Everyone is going to have an opinion, everyone is different.

"We've seen so many epics in five-setters. Do I love five-setters? Absolutely not. There's a lot of times where I'm up two sets to ‌love and I'd love to shake hands and go ​home. But it's tennis, man."

articles.title: US Open: Sky Sports agrees three-year extension to show the US Open until end of 2030
articles.summary: Sky Sports agrees three-year extension to broadcast the US Open; 2026 competition reaches thrilling conclusion at Flushing Meadows this weekend; watch Aryna Sabalenka take on Elena Rybakina in the women's final on Saturday, followed by the men's final on Sunday
articles.body:
As part of the partnership with the United States Tennis Association (USTA), Sky Sports will retain exclusive live coverage of all men's and women's singles, doubles, mixed doubles, juniors and wheelchair competitions throughout the three-week tournament. The agreement was negotiated by the USTA's media rights partner, IMG.

Alongside broadcast rights, fans in the UK and Ireland will also be able to catch up on all the action with clips and highlights available across Sky's digital and social platforms.

This year's coverage has featured augmented reality graphics, enhanced data integrations, in-depth touchscreen analysis and behind-the-scenes content, bringing fans closer to the action than ever before.

Sky's tennis coverage is led by presenter Gigi Salmon and includes expert analysis from Tim Henman and Laura Robson, alongside additional talent and co-commentators at events throughout the season. Match commentary is provided by Jonathan Overend.

The announcement comes amid a drama-filled US Open featuring the shock first-round exit of 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic and the latest finish in tournament history between Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz as the American emerged victorious at 3.33am.

A thrilling women's final meanwhile awaits as World No 1 Aryna Sabalenka takes on World No 2 Elena Rybakina on Saturday.

Jonathan Licht, Chief Executive Officer Sky Sports UK & Ireland, said : "The US Open is one of the highlights of the sporting calendar, featuring the biggest names in both the men's and women's games, all set against the spectacular New York backdrop. We're delighted to extend our partnership with the USTA, reinforcing our shared commitment to embracing innovation, showcasing the best in the sport and delivering world-class coverage for viewers. This renewal further cements Sky Sports' position as the home of sport in the UK and Ireland, offering fans unrivalled breadth and value all year round."

Kirsten Corio, Chief Commercial Officer, USTA: "The US Open and Sky Sports have been trusted partners for many years, and we're excited to continue such a strong relationship with this renewal. Sky shares our commitment to delivering innovative and cutting-edge coverage to a great audience of tennis fans in the U.K. and Ireland, and we're confident that our continued partnership will have a direct impact on tennis' extraordinary growth and deepen fans' connection with the game."

Live tennis is available all year on Sky, including full coverage of the ATP and WTA Tours on Sky Sports or available to stream with NOW and the Sky Sports app. Sky Sports will broadcast over 4,000 matches and 80 tournaments this season.

The partnership extension adds to Sky's already unrivalled portfolio in the UK and Ireland with more top-quality sport than anywhere else, with most sport rights renewed until near the end of the decade. That includes 1,500 games from the Premier League, WSL, EFL and SPFL, exclusive live coverage from every Formula 1 race weekend until the end of 2034, home men's and women's international England cricket, every shot from the golf Majors, year-round coverage of darts, world class boxing from promoters Zuffa and MVP, and more action from the NFL, Netball Super League and rugby league.

articles.title: US Open: Ben Shelton takes down Frances Tiafoe to seal Alexander Zverev showdown in final on Sunday in New York
articles.summary: Ben Shelton wins all-American duel with Frances Tiafoe to set up US Open final with top seed Alexander Zverev on Sunday; watch the US Open women's final live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app on Saturday from 9pm
articles.body:
On a poignant evening that began with commemorations marking the 25th anniversary of ​the September 11 attacks, Shelton ‌came from a set down to beat Tiafoe 4-6 6-3 6-3 7-5 and move closer ​to ending a 23-year ‌American wait for a men's singles Grand Slam ​champion.

No home male player has won a Grand Slam singles title since Andy Roddick triumphed in Flushing Meadows in 2003. Shelton will now have a chance to claim his maiden Grand Slam crown.

Earlier, Zverev booked his place in the final with a 6-3 7-6 (9-7) 7-6 (8-6) victory against Karen Khachanov to move a step closer to a ‌second Grand Slam title.

Shelton said: "First, 'Foe' is like a big brother to me. This is where we want to be, at the tail end of this tournament.

"I know what my goal is, what my job is. I'm going for it here. Let's do this for the USA!

"One more thing. It's a difficult day to be out here playing. My thoughts and prayers go to all the families who were impacted by 9/11."

Tiafoe ⁠powered ahead 5-4 ⁠when Shelton produced a double fault, before raising the ‌roof with a hold to bag the first set.

Tiafoe ‌continued to target his opponent's backhand in the second set but serving at 2-1, Shelton thought he had clocked the fastest serve in Grand Slam history with a 158 mph bullet. However, Hawk-Eye and the USTA later confirmed through review that it only hit 144 mph.

With new balls at 3-3, Shelton started with a 125 mph serve - Tiafoe got his racket up almost in self-defence and ended up getting knocked backwards to the court - and followed it with serves clocked at 144, 139 and 140, as he dialled up the intensity to draw ⁠level.

He then broke in the ​fifth game of the third ​set to take a commanding ​lead in the match.

With his booming ⁠left-handed serve and his defence proving impenetrable in the high-octane fourth set, ⁠eighth seed Shelton heaped ​the pressure on late to wrap up an emotional win.

The 23-year-old finished with 47 winners, including 20 aces, to book his place in the title match.

Zverev downs Khachanov to close in second major

The French Open champion had been pushed to five sets in ​each of his opening two rounds but has now won four straight matches without dropping a set, as he reached ​his third consecutive major final.

The victory sent him to his second title decider at Flushing Meadows, after finishing runner-up in 2020 to Dominic ​Thiem.

"After the second round at 3am, me and my team were in the dressing room actually laughing at how bad I was playing. ​That sense of humour helped me," Zverev said ⁠on court.

"I have improved a little ⁠bit, otherwise I wouldn't be in the US Open final."

The German had played all his previous matches during the night sessions, existing in a perpetual loop of darkness and midnight finishes.

The 29-year-old has capitalised on the absence of Jannik Sinner and defeats for Carlos Alcaraz and Novak Djokovic, as well as a kind draw, to reach a third consecutive Grand Slam final.

"I really started off the tournament, and I ​was like, 'Well, this is pointless because I'm not going to do anything here,' and here I am sitting and preparing for a Sunday final," Zverev ​told reporters.

A solitary break was all Zverev needed to pinch a tight first set from his opponent and when he broke again at start of the second, a routine afternoon looked on the cards.

However, a double fault allowed Khachanov back on serve and instead Zverev became embroiled in a tie-break, at one point trailing 5-3 and only winning it after a lung-busting 35-shot rally.

The third set went the same way and Khachanov had set points at 6-4, but two wayward forehands and a Zverev ace gave him match point, which he took at the first attempt.

Rather than fearing a partisan crowd on Sunday, Zverev said he was looking forward to it.

"I think it's going to be a fantastic ​feeling playing, you know, a final in a sold-out Arthur Ashe ​and not in an empty one," he said. "For me, a loud and energetic crowd is always great, as long as ‌they're fair."

Navratilova: There are no asterisks in Zverev's successes

"What a year Zverev has had at the majors. It's been outstanding stuff.

"Okay, Sinner lost early at the French Open and Alcaraz didn't play, but there are no asterisks; he still had to get through even as a favourite.

"And that has given the confidence to play better tennis after that. I think he played better at Wimbledon than he did at Roland Garros, and now he started off badly here by his own admission, but he hasn't lost a set the last four matches.

articles.title: US Open 2026: Brits Neal Skupski, Alfie Hewett clinch respective doubles, wheelchair titles at Flushing Meadows
articles.summary: Britain’s Alfie Hewett regained his US Open wheelchair singles title with victory in Saturday’s final; compatriot Neal Skupski clinched men’s doubles title; watch US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, NOW and Sky Sports app
articles.body:
Emotional Hewett burst into tears after beating Tokito Oda 6-0 7-6 (7-5) to deny the 20-year-old Japanese star a calendar Grand Slam.

The 28-year-old, who was beaten by Oda in the finals of the French Open and Wimbledon this year, said: "It's taken lot of hard work, a lot of soul-searching at times, a lot of reflecting.

"The Wimbledon pumping was a tough one to swallow. I definitely came away from that one with a lot of regret, took some time off and had a hard, long look in the mirror about who I wanted to be on the tennis court and how I wanted to show up.

"Today I didn't care about the outcome. It was about being a little bit more like 'Alfie' and showing the fight and showing the grit and the desire to go out and play a bit more fearless. I think the performance showed that."

It was Hewett's fifth US Open title but his first since 2023, and will sit nicely with the doubles trophy he won with Gordon Reid on Friday.

Skupski and American Christian Harrison beat German duo Kevin Krawietz and Tim Puetz 6-4 7-6 (8-6).

Skupski had twice been runner-up at Flushing Meadows, alongside Wesley Koolhof in 2022 and Britain's Joe Salisbury last year.

Jamie Murray and his American partner Bruno Soares presented the trophies on the 10th anniversary of their win here.

Skupski, 36, said: "I'm still in shock. Losing twice and having match points last year was a tough part of my career, but it's amazing what a year does in tennis.

Harrison and Skupski were competing in just their second tournament together when they won the Australian Open in January. By also claiming Wimbledon, they became the fourth men's doubles team since Melbourne switched to hard courts in 1988 to win both majors in the same year.

"It's been a great year," Harrison said. "To get two titles like this, I'm speechless - and to do it at home."

articles.title: US Open: Elena Rybakina cements her spot as world No 1 by dethroning two-time winner Aryna Sabalenka in New York
articles.summary: Elena Rybakina won her first US Open title and punctuated her climb to the top of women's tennis by beating Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 5-7 6-2 on Saturday; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
Rybakina ​won ‌her ​first US Open, beating top seed ‌and defending champion ⁠Sabalenka ​6-4 ​5-7 ⁠6-2 on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The 27-year-old had already been guaranteed to replace Sabalenka at No 1 in the rankings next week.

Sabalenka was looking to become only the third woman to achieve a New York 'three-peat' in the Open era, after Chris Evert and Serena Williams.

Instead she was left sat in her chair, furiously smashing her racket in to smithereens as Rybakina, from Kazakhstan, celebrated a third Grand Slam title.

An ankle injury ‌had threatened to derail Rybakina's campaign even before the tournament started, but she shrugged off those ​concerns to add the US Open title to her Australian Open triumph this year and Wimbledon success in 2022.

"Some magic is happening," Rybakina told Sky Sports Tennis . "I was so unlucky with the injury [before the start of the tournament]. I was going day by day and my team were quite positive. Even in the beginning we didn't know how it was going to be so I'm super happy and very proud. I still can't believe it.

"I was relieved to get to No 1 but I knew there were two more matches to push and it would be such a milestone winning the tournament here so I was focused and trying not to see too many messages.

The title showdown on a packed Arthur Ashe Stadium had all ​the ingredients of a classic between the top two in the ⁠rankings.

Dressed in a yellow-and-black outfit that evoked a bee, Rybakina ‌produced some stinging groundstrokes but was unable to make the early pressure count as Sabalenka unleashed big serves to hold firm in the pair's third Grand Slam final ‌meeting.

The second seed drew first blood to go ahead 3-2 following a Sabalenka double fault, with the frustrated Belarusian earning a code violation immediately afterwards for launching a ball high into the stands.

Sabalenka's irritation became increasingly evident with each ⁠missed shot and squandered opportunity, in stark contrast to the trademark ​calm etched on Rybakina's face as the Kazakh tightened her ​grip on the opening set and clinched it with a tight ​hold.

A sudden drop-off in Rybakina's level midway through the second set gave the ⁠28-year-old Sabalenka hope, and she produced a stunning drop shot and a backhand crosscourt winner en route to forcing a deciding set.

Sabalenka let out a huge roar after another ⁠backhand winner to hold in a tight opening ​game of the third set.

However, Rybakina's quality shone through her red-and-blue-framed racket ​as she took a commanding 5-2 lead and then closed out a famous triumph to leave her Belarusian rival without any ‌major silverware in 2026.

Sabalenka said: "The last thing I want to do right now is give a speech, but I'll try my very best. Thank you everyone. Thank you for all your support.

"I want to congratulate Elena on an incredible year, an incredible result. Well deserved. Enjoy it tonight, and have fun. So I can win some titles!

"I wish I could have performed a little bit better, but I guess there's next year."

She later spoke about smashing a ball into the crowd and breaking a racket during her press conference, saying: "It's really tough to control your emotions when you lose in the final of the Grand Slam and when you were trying to go for three-peat.

"I just wanted to let it go, because if I would hold it inside, right now or here or there on the court, I wouldn't be able to say a word or I would just go not really nice over there. I just wanted to let all of that aggression and disappointment go outside."

Navratilova: Sabalenka simply did not know what to do - she usually dominates!

"We do not see that. Usually it's Sabalenka doing the bullying.

"I think that's why Sabalenka didn't know what to do. She's used to dictating, to putting people on the defence, on their heels and rushing shots.

"Instead, it was all Rybakina doing that to her. And I did not expect that.

"It's not that Sabalenka lost the match, Rybakina won it. She earned that win.

"It will be back to the drawing board for Sabalenka. What will she do next time if Rybakina is playing this well?"

Bartoli: Extraordinary Rybakina can do anything on a tennis court

"Can you imagine that her previous best result here was the fourth round?

"That's extraordinary, to come here with all the pressure of the world, knowing she had the No 1 world ranking on her racket, to actually go on and win the title.

"The way she bounced back at the beginning of the third set tonight for me, was absolutely extraordinary.

"It looked like she completely forgot what happened at the back end of that second set, when she got caught on her own service game.

"She just kept on moving on, and moving forward all the time. The way she attacked Sabalenka's serve all the time, putting her under so much pressure.

"The ball-striking from that young lady is just something else. She can do anything on the tennis court.

"She's only missing Roland Garros now from completing a career Grand Slam."

Robson: Key difference was Rybakina's lights out backhand

"We were excited about this final for good reason. Because of how well we know both of these players perform on big occasions like this.

"For Rybakina, without even crowd support on her side, she just did not flinch.

"Yes, you could maybe point to the double faults at the end, but under so much pressure, and Sabalenka trying everything to make a comeback in that third set, she just kept going for her shots.

"It is just unbelievable how hard both of these players hit the ball. Their timing is phenomenal.

"The difference today was the backhand from Rybakina, which was lights out from start to finish."

articles.title: US Open: Top seed Alexander Zverev ends Ben Shelton’s run and American dreams to claim title in four sets
articles.summary: Alexander Zverev adds a maiden US Open title to his French Open crown after overcoming Ben Shelton in a four-set battle; watch the Laver Cup at The O2 in London from 25-27 September live on Sky Sports.
articles.body:
The German proved too strong for the eighth-seeded American prevailing 6-3 7-6 (7-2) 5-7 6-2 in the final at Flushing Meadows.

Zverev added the New York title to his collection after winning the French Open earlier this year. In a bizarre ending, Shelton's return sailed long on match point, but Zverev, seemingly unaware that he had won, hit the balls back to the other end of the court, ready for another game.

It was only when Zverev glanced up at the big screen that he realised he had actually won.

"I feel like there was so much suffering for the Zverev family at Grand Slam level, that maybe 2026 is the year we should just enjoy," Zverev told Sky Sports Tennis . "Everything is going perfectly. I am unbelievably happy.

"Three months ago if I was told you are going to win one Grand Slam in your career and nothing else, I would have signed the paper straight away and never questioned it.

"Now standing here with two Grand Slam trophies in the space of the months is incredible."

And on not realising he had won it on Championship point, he admitted: "I thought the score was 5-1! I knew that I had broken him twice, but I thought he only held once.

"I was thinking: 'Okay, I'm going to have a relaxed service game here and then I'll get tight on the next one.' "It was lucky for me!

"It's actually funny, teachers in tennis say play each point and forget about the score. Well I forgot about the score and it helped me!"

Shelton was bidding to become the first American man to win a Grand Slam singles title since Andy Roddick in 2003, while also aiming to become only the second black man to triumph at this level after Arthur Ashe in 1975. He walked onto the court to a rapturous reception from a partisan crowd of 23,000 spectators inside the stadium named in Ashe's honour.

Among the star-studded crowd were actors Brad Pitt and Rami Malek, as well as James Bond star Pierce Brosnan, who received a mischievous camera shot from the TV director with the match clock showing just 0.07.

Despite spending 19 hours and 38 minutes on court en route to the final - the fourth-longest total recorded by a player reaching a Grand Slam final since 1991 - Zverev made a blistering start. He broke in the opening game and then broke again on set point to seize control.

Shelton could not even earn a break point in the opening two sets, as Zverev, the No 1 seed at a Grand Slam for the first time, relied on his powerful serve to keep the American at bay.

Shelton had lost all five of his previous meetings with Zverev, but he had also arrived in New York having never beaten Stefanos Tsitsipas or, most notably, Carlos Alcaraz - until this tournament. That run gave him plenty of reason for optimism heading into Sunday's final at Flushing Meadows.

But Zverev, now playing with freedom after shedding the unwanted tag of the 'best player never to win a major' with his French Open triumph earlier this year, dominated the second-set tie-break to move within touching distance of the title.

Shelton dug in, to his credit, and finally brought up three break - and set - points as the Zverev serve suddenly faltered, and the crowd were in full voice again when he converted the second.

But the match was effectively over as a contest when Zverev, who has capitalised on the fitness struggles and absences of Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner at various points this year, broke early in the fourth set.

His incessant ball-bouncing - statistics showed he spent around three hours of his 23-plus hours on court this fortnight bouncing the ball between serves - finally resulted in a time violation.

Meanwhile, Shelton's girlfriend Trinity Rodman pulled off a logistical miracle, making the 200-mile trip from a football pitch in Washington to Queen's, arriving in time to slip into her other half's box.

But it proved to be a wasted trip as Zverev held his nerve to clinch Grand Slam title No 2, and his first in New York, in three hours and 33 minutes. After a brief pause to take it all in, he finally began to celebrate.

Shortly after his victory, Zverev reserved his most heartfelt thanks for his mother Irina, a former professional tennis player, crediting her with ​refusing to let type 1 diabetes dictate his future.

"When your four-year-old son is diagnosed ⁠with diabetes and doctors in the office tell you ⁠that life and sports will be very limited for that child, it takes a very strong mother to say 'my son will be whatever he wants ‌to be'," Zverev said.

"If he wants to be a tennis player, he'll be a tennis player. If he wants to do something else, he'll do something else but this illness will not define us.

"I'm happy ‌that we worked through it and we're doing things that we're doing right now. My mother is the most important and strongest person I know because it takes an unbelievably strong woman to do what she did."

Zverev also paid tribute to Shelton, saying: "Ben, you're an incredible player and an incredible person.

"This was your first Grand Slam final but I already told you you're going ​to be back here many more times and if I would have to bet all my money on it, I would bet that you would lift this ‌trophy one day."

Shelton, who was not even a year old the last time an American man won a Grand Slam title, said: "Sascha, congrats on these two weeks, your second Grand Slam title and two in one year.

"What you're doing is incredible, the way you are serving and moving in play. You work harder than anyone I know, and do more hours on court than anyone else.

"You and your team do things the right way and I'm sincerely happy for you guys to hold this title.

"To New York, you guys drove me here today. I'm just getting started and I'll be back here again."

Henman: Zverev has transformed from a player who was going backwards a year ago

"The perseverance and the way Zverev's game has improved over the last 12 months," said the former British No 1.

"I was looking back at his Grand Slam results, and his game was going backwards.

"But he has transformed himself to be more aggressive, and when you reflect on this matchup, Zverev had beaten Shelton five times in a row.

"Shelton had to change the narrative, but Zverev looked so comfortable.

"Shelton did a great job getting that third set, but losing his serve first game of the fourth settled Zverev down and gave him more energy. He coasted to the line from there."

Bartoli: Difference in experience was massive factor

"The difference in their experience was absolutely massive," said the former Wimbledon champion.

"When you look at the first game of the final, Ben Shelton won the toss, elected to serve, fell to 30-30, missed an easy shot and then double faulted to give away the first break straight away.

"Look, it's not easy to come out in front of your home crowd and play your first ever Grand Slam final in those circumstances.

"Of course you have all the crowd for you, but you want to please them at the same time, put on a show and play your best tennis.

"Zverev made only one unforced error in the first set, and it just made Shelton's life so difficult.

"There's no shame losing to Zverev when Zverev is playing like this."

articles.title: US Open: Alexander Zverev sends out warning to Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, claiming he is currently the best tennis player in the world
articles.summary: Alexander Zverev claims he is currently the best player in the world following his victory at the US Open over American hope Ben Shelton; you can also watch the Laver Cup at The O2 in London from 25-27 September live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
‌German Zverev beat Ben Shelton in the final on Sunday to the bitter disappointment of the home crowd in ‌New York.

Zverev was playing in his sixth major final and Shelton his first, and it showed in a 6-3 7-6 (7-2) 5-7 6-2 victory that extinguished America's hopes of a first male winner since Andy Roddick in 2003.

The 29-year-old has been the dominant player in Grand Slams in a season that has seen Carlos Alcaraz, who won this year's Australian Open, exit the US Open in a quarter-final defeat by Shelton after a long injury lay-off while world No 1 Jannik Sinner pulled out injured before the tournament began after winning Wimbledon.

Zverev finally broke through to win his first major at the French Open, then reached the final at the All England Club, losing to Sinner.

He is 25-2 in Grand Slam matches in 2026 and Zverev believes he is currently the best in the world.

"You have to take everything into consideration," he said. "With Jannik Sinner being injured and Carlos Alcaraz coming back from injury after four months, right now, probably yes. Both of them healthy and both of them at the top of their game, maybe not.

"But if we say right, right now with Jannik being injured and Carlos coming back from injury, maybe. I mean, four, five months ago when both of them were healthy, I wasn't. I was losing to Jannik all the time. So if everyone is healthy, I think Jannik is still ahead. It's as simple as that."

Zverev: I forgot about the score and it helped me

Zverev was so focused on the job ​at hand, he did not even realise he had won the title when Shelton smacked a service return long.

As the umpire announced 'Game, set and match Zverev', the German headed back to the baseline, ready to receive Shelton's serve.

It took him a few seconds to register why the cheering fans were giving him a standing ovation - as he belatedly cracked ​a smile and ran to the net to embrace Shelton.

Speaking to Sky Sports Tennis , he said: "I thought the score was 5-1! I knew that I had broken him twice, but I thought he only held once.

Shelton said he was ‌eager to get another taste of the spotlight on tennis' biggest stage.

"It's such a cool moment. Walking out on that court today, there's nothing like it. I've never felt anything like that ‌before. Yeah, it's an addictive feeling being in positions like this," said the 23-year-old.

The USTA previously pointed to Taylor Fritz's 2024 campaign as a sign of progress, after announcing a massive overhaul to its player development programme in 2008.

The sport's ​national governing body has also moved to diversify its talent in ​a partnership announced last year with American Tennis Association, focusing on building Black representation ​in an overwhelmingly white sport.

Shelton made history just by stepping onto the court on ⁠Sunday as the first Black American man to play in the New York final in 54 years - since Arthur Ashe, the man for whom the tournament's showpiece court was named.

"I don't think I'm anywhere near ⁠the player that I want to be. I think ​I'm a great competitor. I think I compete really well out there on the ​court," said Shelton.

"I'm able it stay focused and stay there on the court for many, many hours. I think that's going to help me ‌in the future moving forward."

Henman: Zverev has transformed from a player who was going backwards a year ago

"The perseverance and the way Zverev's game has improved over the last 12 months," said the 2004 US Open semi-finalist.

articles.title: Jack Draper will be sidelined from tennis for the rest of the year as he rules out returning before 2027
articles.summary: Jack Draper's injury woes continue as he rules out a return to action until 2027; the British star has not been able to play in any Grand Slam tournaments this year; "a complicated injury made things incredibly challenging," Draper admitted
articles.body:
In an emotional Instagram post, Draper said he won't be able to play again until 2027.

"Don't usually love lots of words on here but I wanted to update you that I am aiming to return to the tour at the start of 2027," Draper stated.

"Last summer all the dedication and work I had put into this sport was coming together. It was all going my way and the path seemed so clear.

"However a complicated injury made things incredibly challenging and since that moment I've been desperately trying to get back and feel as I once did on the court. Managing so much change, adversity and pain has helped me to grow massively in many areas of my life but has also made me feel a level of fatigue."

He added: "I am taking this time to reset and heal so when I return I am 100% ready to go.

"Tennis is my purpose and passion and so when I step back on court I want to make sure that there's nothing holding me back from where I want to go.

"I really appreciate all the continued support from my sponsors and people who enjoy following my tennis and I look forward to being back on court to give it my all next year."

Draper could not enter the US Open this year as he continued to struggle with a bone bruise in his dominant left arm.

The former world No 4, who has not played at a single Grand Slam this year, said he was in a "difficult place" after his first-round defeat by Martin Landaluce in the Cincinnati Open in August, admitting he was struggling to escape the mental fatigue that had built up during 15 months of battling serious injury.

articles.title: WTA Finals: Charlotte's Spectrum Center revealed as new United States home for showpiece WTA event from 2027 season
articles.summary: Women's tour signs three-year deal to take end-of-season event to the North Carolina from 2027; WTA wants to create "Super Bowl for women's sports"; watch the conclusion of the 2026 WTA season live on Sky Sports Tennis, with the Finals at Indian Wells on November 8-15
articles.body:
As part of the WTA's desire "to build the preeminent championship experience in women's sport", the tour's showpiece season-ending event for the top eight singles players and doubles teams will be staged at Spectrum Center, the home of the NBA's Charlotte Hornets, in 2027-2029.

This year's WTA Finals are taking place in Indian Wells, California in November after the controversial deal to stage the event in Saudi Arabia ended a year early.

"Our ambition is for the WTA Finals to be not only the premier championship in women's tennis, but one of the defining global events in women's sports," said WTA chair Valerie Camillo said.

"We want to create the Super Bowl for women's sports. And not just the competition, but an event that is the annual gathering for women's tennis, women's sports, and women's sport business.

"Audiences are growing, investment is growing, female athletes are increasingly at the center of sports and culture around the world.

"And women's tennis has helped lead and define that progress for more than 50 years. And we believe our biggest championship should reflect the scale of this moment."

Since being held for five consecutive years in Singapore in 2014-2018, the WTA Finals have been staged at six different venues including this year's at Indian Wells.

"The WTA has always owned the WTA finals, but now going forward, we're going to operate it too," Camillo added.

"We're taking control of the creation of the revenues and the controlling of the expenses and the delivery of the entire thing. And that allows us to control our own destiny."

The WTA is also relocating its global headquarters to Charlotte.

"This is a transformational moment for Charlotte and for our organization," said Will Pitts, CEO of the Charlotte Sports Foundation.

"Bringing the WTA Finals to our city is a testament to what Charlotte has become as a world-class sports destination, and we are incredibly grateful to the WTA for their trust and partnership in making this vision a reality.

"None of this happens without the support of our partners at the state, city, and county levels, and we are deeply thankful for their commitment to growing Charlotte's sports footprint."

articles.title: Laver Cup 2026: Schedule, dates, format, players and how to watch or stream Team Europe vs Team World at London's O2 on Sky Sports
articles.summary: Sky Sports will show the Laver Cup live between Friday September 25 and Sunday September 27 as Team Europe face Team World at The O2 in London; Carlos Alcaraz, Alexander Zverev in action; Watch live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
Earlier this year, Sky Sports agreed a deal with Trident8 to show all three days of the Laver Cup from London's O2 Arena this month.

Here's everything you need to know about tennis' exciting team event...

The event is played over three days, with four matches on the first two days consisting of three singles contests and one doubles. Six players from Team Europe and six from Team World make up the event.

Matches on Friday are worth one point, Saturday two points and Sunday three points. The winner is the first team to reach 13 points.

If the points are level at 12-12 at the end of all matches, there will be a fifth match on Sunday (The Decider).

All matches are best-of-three sets, which progress to a deciding tiebreak if the opening two sets are shared.

In terms of how the individual matches are decided, a blind draw is used to confirm Friday's clashes.

For Saturday's matches, one team picks from a blind draw first, and the other team then selects their players to face those drawn out.

For Sunday, the reverse then takes place as the other team selects from a blind draw, and the opposing team picks which players they want to play thereafter.

Each player must play in at least one singles contest over the first two days, and no player can play in more than two singles matches.

Like golf's Ryder Cup, the venue alternates between Europe and elsewhere per each edition. It has been held annually since 2017.

The 2026 Laver Cup is being staged at London's O2, while the 2027 event will be hosted at the Intuit Dome in Inglewood, Los Angeles.

Which players are competing in the 2026 Laver Cup?

Frenchman Yannick Noah and the USA's Andre Agassi are the respective captains. Britain's Tim Henman is Team Europe's vice-captain, while Australia's Pat Rafter is Team World's vice-captain.

Team Europe lineup: Spain's Carlos Alcaraz , Germany's Alexander Zverev , Italy's Flavio Cobolli , Spain's Rafael Jodar , Czech Republic's Jakub Mensik and Norway's Casper Ruud.

Team World lineup: USA's Brandon Nakashima , Australia's Alex de Minaur , USA's Taylor Fritz , USA's Learner Tien , Kazakhstan's Alexander Bublik and Argentina' s Francisco Cerúndolo.

Who are the defending Laver Cup champions?

In 2025, Team World beat Team Europe 15-9 at the Chase Center in San Francisco.

The first day saw Europe 3-1 ahead after singles wins for Ruud over Reilly Opelka and Mensik over Alex Michelsen, and doubles victory for Alcaraz and Mensik over Fritz and Michelsen.

The second day saw domination from Team World, however, as they won all four contests to take a 9-3 lead - De Minaur beating Zverev, Fritz beating Alcaraz, Cerundolo beating Holger Rune and a doubles pairing of De Minaur and Michelsen beating Ruud and Rune.

On the final day, a doubles pairing of Alcaraz and Ruud beat Michelsen and Opelka, and Alcaraz beat Cerundolo in singles, but it wasn't enough as De Minaur beat Mensik and Fritz beat Zverev to wrap up victory.

Henman: Laver Cup a unique opportunity for watching tennis fans

Team Europe vice-captain and Sky Sports Tennis expert Tim Henman said:

"It's a unique opportunity to see the best players in the world coming together to represent Team Europe and Team World at the iconic O2 arena.

"Fans can expect plenty of drama, passion and rivalry, both on and off the court.

"It's great news the Laver Cup will be on Sky Sports."

Hosted by presenter Gigi Salmon, Sky Sports will broadcast all 12 matches across day and night sessions on Friday September 25 and Saturday September 26, followed by a single concluding session on Sunday September 27.

There will also be a reporter on the ground keeping fans abreast of all the news from the weekend's action.

Alongside broadcast rights, fans in the UK and Ireland will also be able to catch up on all the action with clips and highlights available across Sky's digital and social platforms.

articles.body:
The 39-year-old recently dropped as low as No 12 in the world rankings following a shock first-round defeat to Argentina's Mariano Navone at the US Open.

That defeat followed on from a third-round exit in May at the French Open - two underwhelming Grand Slam displays coming either side of a run to the semi-finals at Wimbledon, where he was well beaten in straight sets by eventual champion Jannik Sinner.

Djokovic has not won a Grand Slam title since 2023, going three full calendar years without success.

Returning to the ‌ATP 500 event in Beijing, Djokovic is a six-time winner having last competed there in 2015. Sinner won the title last year, but is currently out with a knee injury.

Defeat to Navone in New York marked the first time Djokovic had lost an opening round contest at a Grand Slam since the 2006 Australian Open.

"I am excited to come back and perform in front of all of you at the National Tennis Centre - one of the nicest venues we have in tennis," Djokovic said on an Instagram story on Wednesday.

Also on Wednesday, news came that Britain's Emma Raducanu has withdrawn from this month's China Open and will not return to action until October at the earliest.

Raducanu has not played since losing the Queen's Club final in June, missing Wimbledon and the US Open due to a stress fracture in her leg.

articles.body:
Samuel beat Andres Andrade 4-6 6-4 6-1 in the opening match before Wimbledon semi-finalist Fery defeated Alvaro Guillen Meza 7-5 6-0.

Great Britain are now one win away from the Davis Cup Final 8.

On Sunday, Great Britain duo Henry Patten and Neal Skupski will take on Gonzalo Escobar and Diego Hidalgo in the doubles where they could secure their passage into the knockout stage for the first time since 2023.

On the eve of the tie Cameron Norrie, their only remaining experienced singles player in the absence of Jack Draper, was ruled out with an arm injury.

Fery had marked his debut in the competition a year ago with victory over Poland's Olaf Pieczkowski.

He is now ranked 36th and followed up his brilliant run to the last four at Wimbledon as a wild card by reaching his first ATP Tour final in the US last month.

Following the win, Fery said: "It was awesome. You get goosebumps walking out. It was great playing here, obviously in London, a lot of support from everyone.

"It's always different playing Davis Cup. You're playing for a whole nation, there's more responsibility on your shoulders. It's a weight that I can carry and I felt confident out there."

Samuel, who lost the opening four games before clawing back against Ecuador's number one, said: "That's definitely the most nerves I've had before a match, even more than the slams I've played.

"I obviously didn't start off as good as I wanted to and I went down, but I was like, 'you're a good player, I keep playing my game and I keep believing and get myself going a bit and it will come', and it did in the end.

"It's even better than I thought. The feeling you get when you get the win for your country is something I've never felt like I've experienced before."

Germany are currently level with Croatia at 1-1, Austria lead Belgium 3-1, South Korea lead India by the same scoreline, while Canada lead France 2-0. Spain lead Chile 2-0.

articles.title: World Team Cup: Alfie Hewett and Gordon Reid win fifth title for Great Britain
articles.summary: Great Britain become World Team Cup champions for the fifth time as Alfie Hewett and Gordon Reid secure a 2-1 victory over Japan in Florida.
articles.body:
Great Britain became World Team Cup champions for the fifth time as Alfie Hewett and Gordon Reid joined forces to secure a 2-1 victory over Japan in Florida.

Japan were the defending champions of the competition, which is the wheelchair tennis equivalent to the Davis Cup and Billie Jean King Cup.

However, Hewett and Reid ensured Britain got their hands back on the trophy with a 6-1 6-2 win in the deciding doubles match against Tokito Oda and Daisuke Arai.

"We're really happy to get the title back," said Reid, who was also part of the World Team Cup-winning squad alongside Hewett in 2015, 2019, 2023 and 2024 .

Hewett added: "It's the first time it's come down to the deciding doubles for us, so I'm just really happy that we got over the line.

"It's always a privilege to play for your country and there's been a great atmosphere and team spirit again this week between all the lads."

Reid got Britain off to a winning start on Saturday with a commanding 6-2 6-2 victory over world number 21 Arai, who he has now beaten in all five encounters between the pair.

The start of the second singles match was then delayed because of extreme heat in Orlando, with Hewett and Oda returning to court six hours later when temperatures had cooled.

Just a week after beating the world number one in the singles final of the US Open, Hewett was unable to repeat his feat as he fell to a narrow 6-4 7-5 loss.

"I'm a bit disappointed that it wasn't a 100% day after my loss in the singles, but it was a really high-level match and just came down to a few points in both sets that could have gone either way," he said.

However, Hewett bounced back in the doubles alongside Reid as Britain, who also had 21-year-old Ben Bartram in the team and were captained by Martyn Whait, backed up their wins against South Korea and the Netherlands earlier this week.
